Extraction: Event-Driven Agentic SOC (ED-ASOC): Supervisor-Based LLM Framework for Dynamic Incident Response and SOAR Orchestration (title page, p. 1).

SOCs face a widening gap between alert volume and the speed of traditional incident response: high false-positive rates cause analyst cognitive overload, alert fatigue, and missed critical threats (Abstract, p. 1; §I, p. 1). Current SOAR platforms automate routine tasks but depend on polling-based data retrieval (e.g., every 30-60 s) and static, rule-based playbooks that cannot adapt to polymorphic malware, zero-day exploits, or living-off-the-land techniques (§I, p. 1; §III.A, p. 2). The polling delay opens a critical vulnerability window for ransomware and APT lateral movement that can occur within minutes of compromise, and existing AI deployments in security remain passive (query generation, log summarization) — unable to interact with the environment, so every action bottlenecks on human intervention (§I, p. 1).

ED-ASOC, a five-layer event-driven framework (ingestion, reasoning, knowledge management, execution, governance) centered on a Supervisor Agent — an autonomous LLM-powered decision engine with actionable intelligence that interacts directly with firewalls, EDR agents, and identity providers (§I, p. 1; §III, Fig. 1, p. 2). Components: (1) a Webhook push-based ingestion layer replacing periodic polling, SIEM-agnostic (Splunk, ELK, FortiSIEM, Azure Sentinel) via JSON payloads (§III.A, p. 2); (2) the Supervisor Agent's three-stage pipeline — contextual classification by semantic similarity against the RAG knowledge base, severity assessment from asset criticality and organizational risk profiles, and remediation synthesis via structured chain-of-thought — with historical correlation against 2,847 indexed incident patterns (§III.B, pp. 2-3); (3) RAG-enhanced dynamic playbook generation from a vector database of historical incidents, security policies, and SOPs, replacing static if-then logic (§III.C, Table I, p. 3); (4) a SOAR Tool Calling interface with a registry of 47 functions in five categories (network controls, endpoint actions, identity management, ticket operations, forensic collection), each bound to strict JSON schemas with validation, rollback procedures, and atomic execution guarantees (§III.D, Table II, p. 3; §III.E, p. 3); (5) a tiered Human-in-the-Loop mechanism — low-risk actions fully automatic, medium-risk auto with notification, high-risk blocked pending analyst approval with natural-language justification (§III.E, Table III, p. 3). The agentic role is explicitly executive: the agent autonomously performs remediation (IP blocking, endpoint isolation, user suspension, file quarantine) through defined API schemas, closing the detection-to-containment gap (Abstract, p. 1; Table II, p. 3).

Design-and-evaluate study with empirical comparison in a controlled simulated testbed emulating an enterprise SOC: FortiSIEM 7.1.1 on VMware ESXi receiving logs from 12 simulated network segments; FortiSOAR 7.4.1 with custom connectors for firewall, EDR, and Active Directory; Claude 3.5 Sonnet as LLM backend (average response latency 1.2 s); Chroma DB holding 2,847 historical incident records and 156 organizational policy documents (§IV.A, p. 3). Synthetic dataset of 1,247 security events across five MITRE ATT&CK categories — Brute Force T1110 (312; 25.0%), Phishing T1566 (287; 23.0%), Lateral Movement T1021 (198; 15.9%), Data Exfiltration T1041 (243; 19.5%), Privilege Escalation T1068 (207; 16.6%) — injected with randomized Poisson timing (λ = 4.2 events/minute) (§IV.B, p. 3). Two executed baselines: a polling-based configuration and a non-agentic LLM-Assist baseline using the same underlying LLM for advisory analysis only, with analysts manually implementing recommended actions (§IV.C, pp. 3-4; Table IV, p. 4). Metrics: detection latency, average MTTR, classification accuracy, auto-resolution rate; no statistical significance testing is reported.

Executed empirical comparison against two concrete baselines (satisfies RSL Art. I). MTTD proxy (mean detection latency): 0.85 s for ED-ASOC vs 34.2 s for the polling baseline — a 97.5% reduction — and 33.8 s for LLM-Assist (§IV.C, pp. 3-4; Table IV, p. 4). MTTR: average 71.7 s vs 258.4 s for polling, a 72.3% reduction (§IV.C, p. 3; Table IV, p. 4; §VI, p. 5), and 62.3% reduction relative to LLM-Assist (190.4 s), isolating the agentic action layer's contribution (§IV.C, p. 4; §V.D, p. 5). The Abstract rounds these as '73% reduction in MTTR' and '89% decrease in detection latency' (Abstract, p. 1); the 89% figure matches the Discussion's analytical model (T_proc = 847 ms vs a 60-s polling interval, '89% latency reduction', §V.A, p. 4), while the Results section reports 97.5%. Secondary operational metrics: auto-resolution 45.5% (ED-ASOC) vs 12.3% (LLM-Assist) vs 0% (polling) — a 33.2-percentage-point agentic gain (Table IV, p. 4; §VI, p. 5); classification accuracy 91.3% vs 84.2% vs 78.4% (Table IV, p. 4); Tier-1 analyst intervention reduced by approximately 45% (567/45.5% fully automated, 412/33.0% notification-only, 268/21.5% approval-required events) (§IV.C, p. 4). Caveats: all figures come from 1,247 synthetic events in a simulated single-vendor testbed, and the second-scale MTTR measures machine-speed containment rather than a full organizational incident lifecycle (§IV.A-B, p. 3; §V.D, pp. 4-5).

Field: General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Agent Systems
Extraction: The LLM-Assist baseline functions as an ablation separating 'LLM-as-advisor' from 'LLM-as-actor': the LLM backbone alone improves classification (84.2% vs 78.4%) but leaves MTTD/MTTR nearly unchanged (33.8 s latency, 190.4 s MTTR), so the agentic action layer — event-driven ingestion, autonomous tool calling, structured SOAR integration — contributes the majority of operational gains (§IV.C, pp. 3-4; Table IV, p. 4). For safe autonomy, a three-tier validation pipeline (RAG grounding on Chroma DB, JSON schema constraining of every SOAR invocation, semantic consistency check against the alert context) is claimed to achieve 94% hallucination reduction, combining probabilistic reasoning with deterministic safety guarantees (§V.B, p. 4). Latency is formalized as L_total = I_p/2 + T_proc, with event-driven operation collapsing it to T_proc ≈ 847 ms and cutting idle resource consumption by 78% (§V.A, p. 4). Governance data shows calibrated oversight: of 268 high-risk decisions presented, analysts modified 23 (8.6%) and rejected 7 (2.6%) (§IV.C, p. 4). Architecturally the system is single-agent with claimed horizontal scaling beyond 10,000 events/minute behind a load balancer; the authors position a future hierarchical multi-agent design (Orchestrator delegating to Network Forensics, Malware Analysis, and Cloud Security sub-agents with domain-specific RAG bases) to reduce per-agent context-window pressure, extending DeepAgent-style agentic workflow patterns to the security domain (§V.C, p. 4).

Authors acknowledge five limitations (§V.D, pp. 4-5): (1) the single-agent architecture may hit throughput constraints above 10,000 events/minute — to be addressed by hierarchical multi-agent coordination; (2) the RAG knowledge base requires periodic updates — future automated threat-intelligence ingestion pipelines; (3) adversarial robustness against prompt injection targeting the LLM controller remains open, requiring input sanitization and adversarial training; (4) evaluation relies on a synthetic 1,247-event dataset rather than production SOC traffic, so real-world validation is needed to strengthen generalizability; (5) only two baselines were run — intermediate semi-autonomous configurations with selective tool execution would clarify the autonomy-performance tradeoff. Future work also includes privacy-preserving threat-intelligence sharing protocols (§VI, p. 5). Not acknowledged: absence of statistical significance testing, dependence on a single LLM backend (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) and a single-vendor Fortinet stack, and MTTR defined at machine timescale (seconds) in a controlled environment.

Direct and central: ED-ASOC instantiates exactly the thesis object — an agentic LLM copilot/supervisor reducing MTTD and MTTR in incident response — and is one of the four primary studies in the cluster reporting nominal MTTD/MTTR gains against an executed baseline (72.3% MTTR reduction and 97.5% detection-latency reduction vs polling; 62.3% MTTR reduction vs a non-agentic LLM-Assist; §IV.C, Table IV, pp. 3-4). The LLM-Assist ablation is especially valuable for the dissertation's argument, since it quantifies the marginal contribution of agentic autonomy (copilot-as-actor) over advisory LLM use (copilot-as-advisor), and the tiered HITL matrix (Table III, p. 3) plus analyst modification/rejection rates (§IV.C, p. 4) inform the copilot governance discussion. Mandatory stratum caveat: the venue is in the B4 series (PDR-0006/0007), so the evidential weight is discounted accordingly; moreover, all evidence comes from a simulated testbed with synthetic MITRE ATT&CK events, not production SOC traffic (§IV.A-B, p. 3; §V.D, p. 5), so the numbers should be cited as controlled-environment results.

High - the study answers the thesis question head-on with executed baseline comparisons quantifying agentic-copilot reductions in detection latency and MTTR, including an ablation isolating the autonomy layer; weight is tempered by the B4-series venue stratum (PDR-0006/0007) and simulated-testbed-only evidence.
